info.title: Collapse Compression API
info.summary: Asynchronous HTTP compression: upload a file, poll the job, download the archive.
info.description:
Collapse compresses a single uploaded file into a 7z, tar or zip archive. Extraction is not exposed over HTTP; it stays local to the clients.

## The asynchronous flow

Uploading never blocks on the compression itself. A client is expected to walk these four steps in order:

1. **Create the job.** `POST /compress?name=<bare file name>` with the raw file bytes as the request body. The server stages the upload, queues the work and answers `202 Accepted` with a Job whose `status` is `queued`. Keep the `job_id`.
2. **Poll the job.** `GET /jobs/{job_id}` until `status` leaves `queued`/`compressing` and settles on `completed` or `failed`. Polling every 100 to 500 ms is plenty. A `failed` job carries the reason in `error_message`.
3. **Download the archive.** `GET /jobs/{job_id}/download` returns the archive bytes once the job is `completed`, with `Content-Disposition: attachment` naming it `archive_name`. Downloading before the job completes is a `409`. The download may be repeated for as long as the job exists.
4. **Delete the job.** `DELETE /jobs/{job_id}` drops the job and its staged files. Nothing else reclaims that disk space, so always delete after a successful download.

A background worker processes jobs sequentially, so several uploads queue up instead of competing for the CPU. Jobs live in an in-memory registry and their files in a per-job staging directory: nothing survives a server restart.

## Error shape

Errors raised by the application are JSON objects of the shape `{"detail": "<message>"}`. Two rejections are produced by the web framework before the handler runs and are `text/plain` instead: a query string that cannot be deserialized at all (a missing `name`, a non numeric `level`) and a request body over the upload cap. Both are documented on the operations where they can occur.

tags.name: jobs
tags.description: Following a compression job through its lifecycle: poll, download, delete.

get.description: Reports that the server is up and serving. It touches neither the job registry nor the staging directory, so a healthy answer says nothing about pending jobs or free disk space. Use it for load balancer and container health checks.

post.summary: Upload a file and queue a compression job
post.description:
Step 1 of the asynchronous flow. The request body is the **raw bytes of the file** to compress: not multipart, not JSON, not base64. Everything else travels in the query string.

The server validates the parameters, writes the upload to the job's staging directory, registers the job and hands it to the background worker, then answers `202 Accepted` immediately with the job in its `queued` state. Compression has not started yet when the response arrives, so the job in the body always reads `"status": "queued"` and `"error_message": null`.

Exactly one file goes into the archive, stored under `name`. The archive itself is named `archive_name`, which is `<name>.<extension>` for the chosen algorithm. An empty body is accepted and produces an archive holding an empty file.

Continue with `GET /jobs/{job_id}` to poll the job.

**Directories.** HTTP has no notion of a folder, so a client packs one into a tar and sets `envelope=tar`; the server unpacks it and compresses the tree, giving the same archive a local run would produce. Tar is the envelope because it does not compress: the CPU work still happens here, and the upload cap still bounds how much can be unpacked.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: File name the uploaded bytes will carry inside the archive, and the stem of the archive's own name. It must be a bare file name: not empty, not `.`, not `..`, and free of `/`, `\` and NUL bytes. A backslash is rejected even on Unix, where it is a legal filename character, because these archives are opened on Windows too. Anything else is a `400`, since this value is used both as the archive entry name and as the leaf of the staging path.

parameters.name: algorithm
parameters.description: Archive format to produce. Matched exactly and case sensitively, so `ZIP` is rejected. Defaults to `zip`, like the CLI.

parameters.name: level
parameters.description: Compression level, from 1 (fastest, largest) to 5 (slowest, smallest). Defaults to 3, like the CLI. `tar` stores without compressing and ignores the value, but still rejects one outside 1 to 5. A value out of range is a JSON `400`; a value that is not an integer at all is a plain text `400` from the query string parser, never silently coerced to the default.

parameters.name: envelope
parameters.description: Whether the body is a plain file (`none`, the default) or a tar holding one directory to unpack and compress as a tree (`tar`). With `tar`, send the directory's own name as `name`: the tar's single top-level entry must match it, and the archive is named after it.

requestBody.description: The raw bytes of the file to compress, sent as the whole request body. Send an empty body to archive an empty file. Bodies larger than the server's upload cap (500 MiB by default, set with `--max-upload-mb`) are rejected with `413`.

202.description: The upload was staged and the job queued. Compression runs in the background; poll `GET /jobs/{job_id}`.

400.description: The request was rejected before any work was queued. Two different bodies are possible. Validation performed by the handler (an unknown `algorithm`, a `level` outside 1 to 5, a `name` that is not a bare file name) answers with the JSON error shape. Failures of the query string parser itself (`name` missing entirely, `level` not an integer) answer with plain text, because they happen before the handler runs.

value.detail: Invalid compression level: 6. Must be between 1 and 5.
Invalid file name: "../evil.txt". Must be a bare file name.

missingName.summary: name absent from the query string
missingName.value: Failed to deserialize query string: missing field `name`

unparseableLevel.value: Failed to deserialize query string: invalid digit found in string

413.description: The request body exceeded the configured upload cap (500 MiB by default). The limit is enforced while buffering the body, before the handler runs, so the body is plain text rather than the JSON error shape. The query string is parsed first, so a request that is both oversized and malformed answers `400` instead.

tooLarge.value: Failed to buffer the request body: length limit exceeded

500.description: The upload could not be staged on disk, or the job could not be handed to the worker. No job is created.

value.detail: No space left on device (os error 28)

get.description:
Step 2 of the asynchronous flow. Returns the job's current state. Poll this until `status` leaves `queued`/`compressing`.

The lifecycle is `queued` then `compressing` then either `completed` or `failed`, and it never moves backwards. On `completed` the archive is ready at `GET /jobs/{job_id}/download`. On `failed`, `error_message` carries the reason and no archive exists; the job should be deleted.

The job disappears (and this becomes a `404`) once it is deleted or the server restarts.

value.name: notes.txt
value.error_message: Compression failed: unexpected end of file

delete.summary: Delete a job and its staged files
delete.description:
Step 4 and last of the asynchronous flow. Removes the job from the registry and deletes its staging directory, which holds both the upload and the archive. Nothing else reclaims that space, so call this once the archive has been downloaded, and also for jobs that ended `failed`.

It is refused with `409` while the job is `queued` or `compressing`; wait for a terminal state first. After a successful delete every endpoint answers `404` for that `job_id`.

The `deleted` flag in the response reports whether files were actually removed from disk. It is `false` when the job had no staging directory left, for instance if it was already cleaned up externally; the job is dropped from the registry either way.

200.description: The job was dropped from the registry.

nothingOnDisk.summary: Job removed, no files were left to delete

409.description: The job is still `queued` or `compressing`. Poll `GET /jobs/{job_id}` until it is `completed` or `failed`, then retry.

value.detail: Cannot delete a job while compression is in progress.

500.description: The staging directory could not be removed.

get.description:
Step 3 of the asynchronous flow. Streams back the archive bytes for a `completed` job.

The response `Content-Type` follows the job's `algorithm`: `application/zip` for zip, `application/x-7z-compressed` for 7z, `application/x-tar` for tar. `Content-Disposition` suggests the file name from the job's `archive_name`, with the characters that could break out of the quoted value stripped.

The download is idempotent and may be repeated until the job is deleted. Calling it too early is a `409`, not a wait: poll `GET /jobs/{job_id}` first. Finish with `DELETE /jobs/{job_id}`.

200.description: The archive bytes. Which of the three media types is used depends on the job's `algorithm`.

Content-Disposition.description: Always `attachment`, with `filename` set to the job's `archive_name`. Double quotes, backslashes and newlines are stripped from the name so they cannot break out of the quoted value.

404.description: Either no job carries this `job_id` (unknown, already deleted, or lost to a restart), or the job exists and reports `completed` but its archive is gone from the staging directory.

archiveMissing.summary: Job is completed but its file is gone

409.description: The job is not downloadable. While it is `queued` or `compressing` the detail is a fixed message and the client should keep polling. Once it is `failed` the detail is the job's own `error_message`, so the text varies; it falls back to `Compression failed.` when no message was recorded.

failedJob.summary: Job failed, the detail is its error_message

value.detail: Compression failed: unexpected end of file

JobId.name: job_id
JobId.description: Identifier returned in the `job_id` field of the `202` response to `POST /compress`. Any string is accepted by the router; one that matches no job answers `404`.

JobNotFound.description: No job carries this `job_id`. It was never created, it was already deleted, or the server restarted (jobs are held in memory only).

Algorithm.title: Algorithm
Algorithm.description: Archive format. `7z` and `zip` compress and honour `level`; `tar` only bundles the file without compressing it.

Envelope.description:
How the request body should be read. `none` means the body is the file to compress, as it is. `tar` means the body is a tar holding exactly one directory, which the server unpacks and compresses as a tree.

The flag is required rather than inferred: a `.tar` upload may equally be a file the caller wants compressed as itself, and guessing would make that impossible to ask for.

JobStatus.title: JobStatus
JobStatus.description: Lifecycle state of a compression job. It advances `queued` to `compressing` to either `completed` or `failed`, and never moves backwards. `completed` and `failed` are terminal: only then may the job be downloaded or deleted.

Job.title: Job
Job.description: One compression job. Returned by `POST /compress` (always `queued`) and by `GET /jobs/{job_id}` (any state).

job_id.description: Server generated identifier: a version 4 UUID in its 32 character hexadecimal form, without dashes. Use it in every follow up call.

name.description: The `name` query parameter as given: the file name stored inside the archive.

archive_name.description: Name of the produced archive, `<name>.<extension>` for the chosen algorithm. It is what `Content-Disposition` suggests on download.

level.description: Compression level in effect, defaulting to 3. Recorded even for `tar`, which ignores it.

envelope.description: How the upload was read for this job.

error_message.description: Why the job failed. Always `null` unless `status` is `failed`.
examples: Compression failed: unexpected end of file

job_id.description: The job that was dropped from the registry.

deleted.description: Whether the job's staging directory existed and was removed. `false` means there was nothing left on disk; the job is gone from the registry either way.

status.description: Always the literal `ok`. The endpoint has no unhealthy response: a failing server does not answer at all.

Error.title: Error
Error.description: Every error raised by the application uses this shape. The two rejections produced by the web framework before the handler runs (an unparseable query string, an oversized body) are plain text instead.

detail.description: Human readable explanation of what went wrong. The wording is not a stable contract; branch on the status code, not on this text.
